name: Wire or metal utility shelving
tagline: Four posts, plastic sleeves that act as a collar, and shelves that wedge down onto them. No tools, no screws.
peopleNote: One person, though the final shelf is easier with two.

tools.why: The only tool. Shelves wedge onto the posts and need firm taps to seat.
Wire shelf edges and cut post ends are sharp.

before: Decide your shelf heights before you start. Changing one later means lifting every shelf above it off.
Think about what goes on the bottom shelf and leave enough space for it. People always leave too little.
If you want casters, fit them instead of the feet — the posts take one or the other, not both.
safety: Loaded wire shelving in a garage can be very heavy. Tall units should be strapped to the wall.
Never climb on wire shelving. The shelves hold weight but the wedge joints are not designed for a point load at the edge.

steps.title: Understand the sleeve trick
steps.say: Each post is grooved every inch. Two plastic half-sleeves clip around a groove to form a tapered collar. The shelf then wedges down onto that collar. That is the whole system.
do: Look at the numbered grooves running up each post
Notice the plastic sleeves come in matching halves
The sleeve is tapered: wide end up
steps.tip: Once you see that the sleeve is a tapered collar and the shelf is a wedge, everything about these racks makes sense.

steps.title: Fit the feet or casters to the posts
steps.say: Screw a leveling foot into the bottom of each post, or press in the casters if you want it to roll. One or the other.
do: Thread the feet in, a few turns, leaving room to adjust later
Casters press in until they click
Note which end of the post is the bottom — it is usually unthreaded at the top
steps.watch: Casters make a tall loaded rack much less stable. For a garage rack carrying real weight, use the feet.

steps.title: Clip sleeves on at the height of the bottom shelf
steps.say: Pick the groove number for your bottom shelf and clip a pair of sleeves around that groove on all four posts. The same number on all four. This is the only thing you can get wrong.
do: Choose a numbered groove
Snap both sleeve halves around it
Repeat at the identical number on all four posts
steps.tip: Say the number out loud as you do each post. Mismatched sleeve heights are the only failure mode of this entire design.
steps.watch: The tapered sleeve has a wide end and a narrow end. Wide end up, every time, or the shelf will not wedge.

steps.title: Drop the bottom shelf on and tap it down
steps.say: Lower the shelf so its four corner collars sit over the sleeves, then tap each corner down with the mallet until it stops moving.
do: All four corners over their sleeves
Tap each corner in turn, working around
It should feel completely solid when seated
steps.tip: Tap in a circuit rather than hammering one corner fully first. That keeps the shelf level as it wedges.

steps.title: Stand it up on the bottom shelf
steps.say: With the bottom shelf on, stand the frame up. It will now stand by itself, which makes the rest easy.
do: Lift from two opposite posts
Stand it on its feet
Check it is roughly where you want it before adding more shelves
steps.watch: A frame with only one shelf is still floppy. Lift it by the posts near the shelf, not by the top of the posts.

steps.title: Add the rest of the shelves, top one last
steps.say: Work upward: sleeves at a matching number on all four posts, shelf down, tap to seat. Do the top shelf last.
do: Same groove number on all four posts, every time
Shelf down, tap each corner
Leave the tallest gap where your tallest items go
steps.tip: Put the top shelf right at the top of the posts. It braces the frame and stops the posts splaying.

steps.title: Level it and check for rock
steps.say: Push each corner. Turn the leveling foot out on any post that lifts off the floor until the rack sits dead still.
do: Press each top corner to find the short post
Screw that foot out
Recheck all four
steps.tip: A rack that rocks will walk across a garage floor over time as you load and unload it. Level it properly once.

steps.title: Strap a tall one to the wall, then load bottom-heavy
steps.say: Tall racks get a strap to a stud. Then load it with the heaviest things on the bottom two shelves.
do: Strap or bracket at the top, into a stud
Heaviest items lowest
Spread the load across each shelf rather than at one end
steps.tip: Check the per-shelf weight rating in the manual. It is usually generous, but it assumes the load is spread out, not concentrated in one corner.

fixes.a: The sleeves are at different groove numbers. Lift the shelf off, count the grooves on all four posts from the bottom, and set them all identical.

fixes.q: The shelf will not go down onto the sleeve
fixes.a: A sleeve is upside down. They are tapered — the wide end goes up so the shelf collar can wedge onto it.

fixes.q: I need to change a shelf height
fixes.a: Lift off every shelf above it, move the sleeves, and rebuild upward. It is quick but there is no shortcut, which is why choosing heights first matters.

fixes.q: The rack sways side to side
fixes.a: The top shelf is missing or not at the very top of the posts. The top shelf is the brace. Also confirm every shelf corner is fully tapped down.

fixes.q: The posts came in two halves
fixes.a: Many tall racks use threaded post sections that screw together to make a full-height post, or they can be used as two short racks. Both are correct — pick one before you start.
